contenido: 1. The social concern of the Church, aimed at the authentic development of man and society, which respects and promotes the human person in all its dimensions, has always been expressed in very diverse ways. One of the prominent means of intervention has been, in recent times, the Magisterium of the Roman Pontiffs, which, based on the Encyclical Rerum Novarum of Leo Consequently, starting from the invaluable contribution of Leo In this way, he tries to guide men so that they themselves can respond, with the help of reason and human sciences, to their vocation as responsible builders of earthly society.
2. The Encyclical Populorum Progressio,4 which my venerated Predecessor Paul VI published on March 26, 1967, is framed and distinguished within this notable body of social teaching.

3. With this I intend to achieve mainly two objectives of no small importance: on the one hand, to pay tribute to this historic document of Paul VI and the importance of his teaching; on the other, maintaining the line drawn by my venerated Predecessors in the Chair of Peter, to affirm once again the continuity of social doctrine along with its constant renewal. Indeed, continuity and renewal are proof of the perennial validity of the Church's teaching.

4. Convinced that the teachings of the Encyclical Populorum Progressio, addressed to men and society in the 1960s, retain all their force as a call to conscience, now, in the final stretch of the 1980s, in an effort to draw the main lines of today's world, "always from the perspective of the inspiring motive, "the development of peoples", still far from being achieved, I propose to prolong its echo, uniting it with possible applications to the current historical moment, as dramatic as that of twenty years ago.

5. Already upon its appearance, Pope Paul VI's document caught the attention of public opinion due to its novelty. It was possible to concretely verify, with great clarity, these characteristics of continuity and renewal, within the social doctrine of the Church. Therefore, the attempt to rediscover numerous aspects of this teaching, through a careful reading of the Encyclical, will constitute the guiding thread of the present reflection.

6. In this fact we must see more than a simple chronological proximity. The encyclical Populorum Progressio is presented, in a certain way, as a document of application of the teachings of the Council. And this is not only because the Encyclical makes continuous references to the conciliar texts,8 but because it is born from the concern of the Church, which inspired all the conciliar work - particularly the Pastoral Constitution Gaudium et Spes - in the work of coordinating and developing some themes of its social teaching.

7. But also in thematic order, the Encyclical, following the great tradition of the social teaching of the Church, directly proposes the new exposition and the rich synthesis, which the Council has elaborated in a particular way in the Constitution Gaudium et spes. Regarding the content and themes, once again proposed by the Encyclical, it is worth highlighting: the awareness of the duty that the Church, "expert in humanity", has to "scrutinize the signs of the times and interpret them in the light of the Gospel"; 10 the equally profound awareness of its mission of "service", distinct from the function of the State, even when it is concerned with the fate of specific people; 11 the reference to the striking differences in the situation of these same people; 12 the confirmation of the conciliar teaching, a faithful echo of the secular tradition of the Church, regarding the "universal destiny of goods"; 13 appreciation for culture and technical civilization that contribute to the liberation of man,14 without failing to recognize its limits; 15 and finally, on the theme of development, typical of the Encyclical, the insistence on the "very grave duty", which concerns the most developed nations.16 The very concept of development, proposed by the Encyclical, arises directly from the imposition that the pastoral Constitution gives to this problem.17

8. The brief analysis carried out helps us to better assess the novelty of the Encyclical, which can be articulated in three points. The first is constituted by the very fact of a document issued by the highest authority of the Catholic Church and intended both for the Church itself and "for all men of good will",18 on a matter that at first glance is only economic and social: the development of peoples. Here the word "development" comes from the vocabulary of the social and economic sciences. In this aspect, the Encyclical Populorum Progressio is immediately placed in line with Rerum Novarum, which deals with the "situation of the workers."19 Seen superficially, both issues could seem foreign to the legitimate concern of the Church considered as a religious institution. "Development" even more so than the "worker condition."

9. The second point is the novelty of the Populorum Progressio, as manifested by the breadth of horizon, open to what is commonly known under the name of "social question." In reality, the Encyclical Mater et Magistra of Pope John XXIII had already entered into this broader horizon 21 and the Council, in the Pastoral Constitution Gaudium et spes, had echoed it. 22 However, the social magisterium of the Church had not yet managed to affirm with complete clarity that the social question has acquired a global dimension, 23 nor had it managed to make this affirmation and its analysis a "guideline for action", as Pope Paul VI does in his Encyclical.

10. As a third point, the Encyclical provides a considerable contribution of novelty to the social doctrine of the Church as a whole and to the very conception of development. This novelty is found in a phrase that is read in the final paragraph of the document, and which can be considered as its recapitulating formula, in addition to its historical importance: "development is the new name for peace."27

11. The fundamental teaching of the Encyclical Populorum Progressio had great echo in its day due to its novelty. The social context in which we live today cannot be said to be exactly the same as that of twenty years ago. This is why I want to stop, through a brief exposition, on some characteristics of today's world, in order to deepen the teaching of Paul VI's Encyclical, always from the point of view of the "development of peoples."
12. The first aspect to highlight is that the hope for development, so alive then, currently appears very far from reality.

13. It cannot be said that these various religious, human, economic and technical initiatives have been superfluous, given that they have been able to achieve some results. But in general, taking into account the various factors, it cannot be denied that the current situation in the world, from the aspect of development, offers a rather negative impression.

14. The first negative observation that must be made is the persistence and sometimes the lengthening of the abyss between the areas of the so-called developed North and the developing South. This geographical terminology is only indicative, since it cannot be ignored that the borders of wealth and poverty cross within the same societies, both developed and developing. Well, just as there are social inequalities reaching levels of misery in rich countries, so, in parallel, in less developed countries, disconcerting and scandalous manifestations of selfishness and ostentation are often seen.

15. The picture drawn above would, however, be incomplete if other equally negative, even more worrying indicators were not added to the "economic and social indicators" of underdevelopment, starting with the cultural level. These are: illiteracy, the difficulty or impossibility of accessing higher levels of education, the inability to participate in the construction of one's own Nation, the various forms of economic, social, political and religious exploitation and oppression of the human person and their rights, discrimination of all kinds, especially the most odious one based on racial difference. If any of these pests are found in some areas of the more developed North, they are undoubtedly more frequent, longer lasting and more difficult to eradicate in developing and less advanced countries.

16. It should be noted that, despite the notable efforts made in the last two decades by the most developed or developing nations, and international organizations, in order to find a way out of the situation, or at least remedy some of its symptoms, conditions have worsened significantly.

17. Although world society offers fragmentary aspects, expressed with the conventional names of First, Second, Third and also Fourth world, its interdependence remains deeper which, when separated from ethical demands, has dire consequences for the weakest. Furthermore, this interdependence, due to a kind of internal dynamic and under the push of mechanisms that cannot help but be described as perverse, causes negative effects even in rich countries. Precisely within these countries are found, although to a lesser extent, the most specific manifestations of underdevelopment. So it should be a known thing that development either becomes a common fact in all parts of the world, or suffers a process of regression even in areas marked by constant progress. This phenomenon is particularly indicative of the nature of authentic development: either all the nations of the world participate in it or it certainly will not be such.
18. Another indicator, common to most nations, is the phenomenon of unemployment and underemployment.

19. Another phenomenon, also typical of the last period – although not found in all places – is undoubtedly also an indicator of the interdependence between developed and less developed countries. It is the question of international debt, to which the Pontifical Commission Iustitia et Pax has dedicated a document.38

20. If we now examine the causes of this serious delay in the development process, verified in a direction contrary to the indications of the Encyclical Populorum Progressio that had raised so many hopes, our attention focuses particularly on the political causes of the current situation.

21. This is verified with a particularly negative effect on international relations, which look at developing countries. Indeed, as is known, the tension between East and West does not in itself reflect an opposition between two different degrees of development, but rather between two conceptions of the very development of men and peoples, so imperfect that they require a radical correction. This opposition is reflected within those countries, thus contributing to widening the abyss that already exists at an economic level between North and South, and which is a consequence of the distance between the two most developed worlds and the least developed ones.

22. Once these considerations are made, it is easier to have a clearer vision of the picture of the last twenty years and better understand the contrasts that exist in the Northern part of the world, that is, between East and West, as not the ultimate cause of the delay or stagnation of the South.

23. The affirmation of the Encyclical Populorum Progressio, that the resources destined for the production of weapons must be used to alleviate the misery of needy populations,41 makes the call to overcome the opposition between the two blocs more urgent.

24. If the production of weapons is a serious disorder that reigns in today's world with respect to the true needs of men and the use of appropriate means to satisfy them, their trade is no less so. Furthermore, regarding this, it is necessary to add that the moral judgment is even more severe. As is known, it is a trade without borders capable of surpassing even those of the blocks. It overcomes the division between East and West and, above all, that between North and South, reaching the various components of the southern part of the world. We are thus faced with a strange phenomenon: while economic aid and development plans come up against the obstacle of insurmountable ideological, tariff and market barriers, weapons of any origin circulate with almost absolute freedom in different parts of the world. And no one ignores – as highlighted in the recent document of the Pontifical Commission Iustitia et Pax on international debt 42 – that in some cases, capital lent by the developed world has been used to buy weapons in the underdeveloped world.

25. In this regard, it is appropriate to make a reference to the demographic problem and the way it is treated today, following what Paul VI indicated in his Encyclical 45 and what I explained more extensively in the Apostolic Exhortation Familiaris consortio.46
26. This predominantly negative overview of the real development situation in the contemporary world would not be complete if it did not point out the existence of positive aspects.

27. The look that the Encyclical invites us to take on the contemporary world makes us realize, above all, that development is not a rectilinear process, almost automatic and in itself unlimited, as if, under certain conditions, the human race was surely marching towards a kind of indefinite perfection.49 This conception âunited with a notion of "progress" with philosophical connotations of an Enlightenment type, rather than with that of "development",50 used in specifically economic-social senseâ now seems to be seriously questioned, especially after the tragic experience of the two world wars, the planned and partly carried out destruction of entire populations and the atomic danger that threatens. A naive mechanistic optimism is replaced by a well-founded concern for the destiny of humanity.

28. But at the same time, the same "economic" or "economist" conception linked to the word development has entered into crisis. Indeed, today it is better understood that the mere accumulation of goods and services, even in favor of a majority, is not enough to provide human happiness. Nor, therefore, do the availability of multiple real benefits, provided in recent times by science and technology, including information technology, bring liberation from any form of slavery. On the contrary, the experience of recent years shows that if all this considerable mass of resources and potentialities, placed at the disposal of man, is not governed by a moral objective and by an orientation that is directed to the true good of the human race, it easily turns against him to oppress him.

29. Therefore, development that is not only economic is measured and oriented according to this reality and vocation of man seen globally, that is, according to one's own internal parameter. This, certainly, needs the created goods and products of industry, constantly enriched by scientific and technological progress. And the ever-new availability of material goods, while satisfying needs, opens new horizons. The danger of consumer abuse and the emergence of artificial needs should in no way prevent the appreciation and use of the new goods and resources placed at our disposal. On the contrary, we must see in it a gift from God and a response to man's vocation, which is fully realized in Christ.

30. According to Sacred Scripture, then, the notion of development is not only "secular" or "profane", but it also appears, although with a strong socioeconomic emphasis, as the modern expression of an essential dimension of man's vocation. Indeed, man has not been created, so to speak, immobile and static. The first presentation that the Bible offers of him certainly describes him as a creature and as an image, determined in his profound reality by the origin and the kinship that constitutes him. But this same thing places in the human being, man and woman, the germ and the requirement of an original task to be carried out, each one separately and also as a couple. The task is to "dominate" the other creatures, "cultivate the garden"; but it must be done within the framework of obedience to divine law and, consequently, in respect for the image received, a clear foundation of the power of dominion, granted in order to its perfection (cf. Gén 1, 26-30; 2, 15 s.; Sab 9, 2 s.).

31. Faith in Christ the Redeemer, while internally illuminating the nature of development, also guides in the task of collaboration. In Saint Paul's Letter to the Colossians we read that Christ is "the firstborn of all creation" and that "everything was created by him and for him" (1, 15-16). In fact, "everything has its consistency in him" because "God saw fit to make all the fullness reside in him and to reconcile all things through him and for him." (Ibid., 1, 20).

32. The obligation to commit to the development of people is not just an individual duty, much less individualistic, as if it could be achieved with the isolated efforts of each person. It is an imperative for each and every one of the men and women, for societies and nations, in particular for the Catholic Church and for the other Churches and Ecclesial Communities, with which we are fully willing to collaborate in this field. In this sense, just as we Catholics invite separated brothers to participate in our initiatives, in the same way we declare ourselves willing to collaborate in theirs, accepting the invitations they have addressed to us. In this search for the integral development of man we can also do a lot with believers of other religions, as is actually already being done in various places. Indeed, cooperation for the development of the whole man and of each man is a duty of all towards all and, at the same time, it must be common to the four parts of the world: East and West, North and South; or, to the various "worlds", as they say today. Otherwise, if you try to do it in a single part, or in a single world, it is done at the expense of the others; and where it begins, it hypertrophies and perverts by not taking others into account. Peoples and Nations also have the right to their full development, which, although it implies - as has been said - the economic and social aspects, must also include their cultural identity and openness to the transcendent. Not even the need for development can be taken as a pretext to impose one's own way of life or religious faith on others.
33. A type of development that did not respect and promote human rights, personal and social, economic and political, including the rights of Nations and peoples, would not be truly worthy of man.

34. The moral character of development cannot dispense with respect for the beings that constitute visible nature and that the Greeks, referring precisely to the order that distinguishes it, called the "cosmos." These realities also demand respect, by virtue of a triple consideration that deserves careful reflection.

35. In light of the same essential moral character, typical of development, we must also consider the obstacles that oppose it. If during the years that have passed since the publication of the Encyclical this development has not occurred - or has occurred in a scarce, irregular, if not contradictory manner - the reasons cannot only be economic. We have already seen how political motivations also intervene. The decisions that accelerate or slow down the development of people are certainly political in nature. And to overcome the perverse mechanisms that we indicated above and replace them with new ones, more just and in accordance with the common good of humanity, effective political will is necessary. Unfortunately, after having analyzed the situation, we have to conclude that it has been insufficient. In a pastoral document like the present one, an analysis limited only to the economic and political causes of underdevelopment and with due references to the so-called superdevelopment, would be incomplete. It is, therefore, necessary to identify the moral causes that, at the level of the conduct of men, considered as responsible people, put a brake on development and prevent its full realization. Likewise, when scientific and technical resources are available that, through the necessary and concrete political decisions, must contribute to finally directing people towards true development, overcoming major obstacles will only be obtained thanks to essentially moral decisions, which, for believers and especially Christians, will be inspired by the principles of faith, with the help of divine grace.

36. Therefore, it must be noted that a world divided into blocks, presided over in turn by rigid ideologies, where instead of interdependence and solidarity, different forms of imperialism dominate, is nothing more than a world subjected to structures of sin. The sum of negative factors, which act contrary to a true awareness of the universal common good and the need to promote it, seems to create, in people and institutions, an obstacle that is difficult to overcome.64 If the current situation is to be attributed to difficulties of various kinds, we must speak of "structures of sin", which - as I have already said in the Apostolic Exhortation Reconciliatio et paenitentia - are based on personal sin and, therefore, Consequently, they are always linked to concrete acts of people, which introduce them, and make their elimination difficult.65 And thus these same structures are reinforced, spread and are the source of other sins, conditioning the behavior of men.

37. Some particular considerations can be added to this generic analysis of a religious order, to indicate that among the opinions and attitudes opposed to the divine will and the good of others and the "structures" they entail, two seem to be the most characteristic: the desire for exclusive gain, on the one hand; and on the other, the thirst for power, with the purpose of imposing one's own will on others. To each of these attitudes we could add, to characterize them even better, the expression: "at any price." In other words, we are faced with the absolutization of human attitudes, with all its possible consequences.

38. This path is long and complex and is also constantly threatened both by the intrinsic fragility of human purposes and achievements, and by the mutability of external circumstances that are so unpredictable. However, it must be undertaken decisively and, where some steps have already been taken, or even a part of it taken, followed to the end. At the level of present consideration, the decision to embark on that path or continue advancing implies above all a moral value, which believing men and women recognize as required by the will of God, the only true foundation of an absolutely binding ethics.

39. The exercise of solidarity within each society is valid only when its members recognize each other as people. Those who count more, by having a larger portion of common goods and services, must feel responsible for the weakest, willing to share with them what they possess. These, for their part, in the same line of solidarity, should not adopt a merely passive or destructive attitude of the social fabric and, although claiming their legitimate rights, they must do what corresponds to them, for the good of all. For their part, intermediate groups should not selfishly insist on their particular interests, but should respect the interests of others.

40. Solidarity is undoubtedly a Christian virtue. Already in the preceding exposition one could glimpse numerous points of contact between it and charity, which is a distinctive sign of the disciples of Christ (cf. Jn 13, 35).

41. The Church has no technical solutions to offer to the problem of underdevelopment as such, as Pope Paul VI already stated in his Encyclical.69 In effect, it does not propose economic and political systems or programs, nor does it express preferences for one or the other, as long as the dignity of man is duly respected and promoted, and it enjoys the necessary space to exercise its ministry in the world. But the Church is "an expert in humanity,"70 and this moves her to necessarily extend her religious mission to the various fields in which men and women carry out their activities, in search of the happiness, although always relative, that is possible in this world, in accordance with their dignity as persons.

42. The social doctrine of the Church, today more than ever, has the duty to open itself to an international perspective in line with the Second Vatican Council,73 the recent Encyclicals,74 and, in particular, the one we commemorate.75 It will not, therefore, be superfluous to examine again and deepen in this light the characteristic themes and orientations dealt with by the Magisterium in these years.

43. This pressing concern for the poor – who, according to the significant formula, are “the poor of the Lord” 80 – must be translated, at all levels, into concrete actions until some necessary reforms are decisively achieved. It depends on each local situation to determine the most urgent ones and the ways to carry them out; But we should not forget those required by the situation of international imbalance that we have described.

44. Development requires above all a spirit of initiative on the part of the same Countries that need it.81 Each of them must act according to their own responsibilities, without expecting everything from the most favored Countries and acting in collaboration with those that find themselves in the same situation. Each person must discover and make the best use of the space of their own freedom. Each one should become capable of initiatives that respond to society's own demands. Each one should also realize their real needs, as well as the rights and duties they have to face. The development of towns begins and finds its most appropriate realization in the commitment of each town to its development, in collaboration with all the others.

45. What has been said cannot be achieved without the collaboration of everyone, especially the international community, within the framework of solidarity that encompasses everyone, starting with the most marginalized. But developing Nations themselves have the duty to practice solidarity among themselves and with the most marginalized countries in the world.

46. Peoples and individuals aspire to their liberation: the search for full development is the sign of their desire to overcome the multiple obstacles that prevent them from enjoying a "more human life."

47. Within the framework of the sad experiences of recent years and the predominantly negative panorama of the present moment, the Church must strongly affirm the possibility of overcoming the obstacles that, by excess or defect, stand in the way of development, and confidence in true liberation. Confidence and possibility founded, ultimately, on the Church's awareness of the divine promise, by virtue of which present history is not closed in itself but open to the Kingdom of God.

48. The Church knows well that no temporal realization is identified with the Kingdom of God, but that all of them only reflect and in a certain way anticipate the glory of that Kingdom, which we await at the end of history, when the Lord returns. But waiting can never be an excuse to ignore men in their concrete personal situation and in their social, national and international life, to the extent that the latter – especially now – conditions the former. Although imperfect and provisional, nothing that can and should be accomplished through the solidarity efforts of all and divine grace at a given moment in history, to make human life "more human", will have been lost or in vain. This is what the Second Vatican Council teaches in a luminous text of the Pastoral Constitution Gaudium et Spes: «For the goods of human dignity, fraternal union and freedom, in a word, all the excellent fruits of nature and of our effort, after having spread them throughout the earth in the Spirit of the Lord and in accordance with his command, we will find them again, cleansed of all stain, illuminated and transfigured, when Christ hands over to the Father the eternal and universal kingdom...; kingdom that is already mysteriously present on our earth."89

49. In this Marian Year, which I have proclaimed so that the Catholic faithful look more and more to Mary, who precedes us on the pilgrimage of faith,90 and with maternal concern intercedes for us before her Son, our Redeemer, I wish to entrust to her and her intercession the difficult situation of the world today, the efforts that are made and will be made, often with considerable suffering, to contribute to the true development of peoples, proposed and announced by my predecessor Paul VI.
